extracted.intended_audience: general public and readers of defense/military news (veterans, DoD stakeholders)
extracted.subtask_short: military news report on CNN retraction
extracted.subtask_description: A single news article reporting the Department of Defense's reaction to CNN's retraction and apology concerning allegations of U.S. use of sarin in 1970 (Operation Tailwind). It summarizes DoD statements, CNN's internal review conclusions, and contextual facts about the operation and its participants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficiency of evidence for serious allegations
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that the U.S. used sarin or any other deadly gas must be supported by sufficient evidence; if evidence is insufficient the report 'cannot be supported.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As CNN President Tom Johnson said, 'There is insufficient evidence that sarin or any other deadly gas was used.' Journals and broadcasters should base such grave allegations on clear, confirmable evidence or retract if that standard is not met.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confirmation of factual claims about individuals (defectors/targets)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reports asserting that specific individuals were targeted or that Americans defected must be confirmable; unconfirmed assertions should not be presented as fact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CNN's review concluded, 'CNN cannot confirm that American defectors were targeted or at the camp as NewsStand reported.' Reporters should verify identities and targeting claims before broadcast/publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corrective action and apology when reporting is unsupported
rubrics_metrics.description: When a news organization finds a broadcast cannot be supported, it should retract the story and apologize to affected parties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CNN issued a retraction and apology to veterans after its in-house review. The article highlights DoD's welcome of that apology as appropriate redress for harmed individuals ('we welcomed CNN's retraction...and the network's apology to veterans').

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of independent/in-house expert review for contested reports
rubrics_metrics.description: Employing independent or in-house expert review (e.g., hiring a media attorney) is a valid mechanism to evaluate contested or high-stakes reports.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CNN called in media attorney Floyd Abrams for its in-house review, which formed the basis of the conclusion that the broadcast 'cannot be supported.' Organizations should use qualified reviewers to assess controversial stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy in reporting operational details
rubrics_metrics.description: Details about military operations (e.g., whether nerve agents were used, what gases were deployed, casualties, mission outcomes) should be accurately reported and corrected if wrong.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The DoD review found 'no sign of sarin or any other nerve agent' and noted the Air Force dropped tear gas to allow evacuation. Accurate characterization of what occurred (tear gas vs nerve agent; number and condition of participants) is essential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding amplification of false claims that harm credibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters should be mindful that unsupported reports can be used by others to make false allegations and can damage national or institutional credibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bacon said the original story 'does not help U.S. credibility' and that 'Iraq made some statements... alleging, falsely, our use of chemical weapons.' Reporting that lacks firm evidence can have geopolitical consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of the human impact on veterans and participants
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporting should consider and minimize harm to veterans and others directly involved; inaccurate reporting can cause feelings of betrayal and personal hurt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DoD spokesman Ken Bacon emphasized veterans felt 'personally betrayed and hurt by the report' and noted the team's bravery and wounds. Newsrooms should weigh reputational and emotional effects on living participants when publishing contested accounts.
